title: Anonymous Classes and Lambdas
summary: Interfaces make it possible to pass behavior as a parameter (Verhalten als Parameter) to an algorithm. Anonymous classes (anonyme Klassen) and lambdas define this behavior directly; they can capture local values while reading current fields of the enclosing object. Functional interfaces and the different meanings of `this` are key building blocks.
keyFacts: `Property.test(Object)` takes an object and returns `true` or `false`.
`CheckArray.check` handles the traversal; `Property.test` handles the selection rule.
`CheckArray.check` immediately returns `true` on the first match; if there is no match, including when the array is empty, it returns `false`.
`new Property() { ... }` defines an unnamed class and creates an object that implements `Property`.
An anonymous class can implement an interface or extend an abstract or concrete class.
Anonymous classes must implement any remaining abstract methods and can have their own fields and methods.
Captured local variables and parameters must be `final` or effectively final; even reassigning the same value is not allowed.
When a reference is captured, the reference variable must be effectively final; the state of the referenced object may still change.
An anonymous object can continue to use local values after the enclosing method has ended.
When accessed through the enclosing object, its instance fields are read at the time of access; changes can therefore affect tests that have already been created.
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method requirement; implemented `default` methods do not count as additional abstract requirements.
`@FunctionalInterface` is optional and lets the compiler check that the interface is a functional interface.
A lambda supplies the behavior for the abstract method of a functional interface.
The target type determines a lambda's parameter and return types; without a target type, the compiler cannot infer them.
For a lambda with one inferred parameter, parentheses are optional; they are required for multiple parameters or explicit types.
An expression body can return the value directly; a block body requires a `return` for a method with a return value.
A functional interface's single abstract method can have multiple parameters.
In an anonymous class, `this` refers to the anonymous class's object; in a lambda, `this` refers to the lexically enclosing object.
Lambdas cannot extend their own class or declare their own instance fields.
In `r != null && ...`, the right-hand expression is not evaluated for `r == null` because of short-circuit evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about functional interfaces are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: They may not contain methods with implementations.
`@FunctionalInterface` is optional.
Their abstract method must have exactly one parameter.
They may also contain a `default` method.
They have exactly one abstract method requirement.

questions.explanation: What matters is that there is exactly one abstract method requirement, not how many parameters it has. Implemented methods such as `default` are also allowed; the annotation is optional.

questions.prompt: For a lambda with one inferred parameter, the parentheses in `___ r != null` are optional.

options.text: `new r =>`
`return r ->`

questions.explanation: The parentheses can be omitted for a single inferred parameter. The arrow separates the parameter list from the lambda body.

questions.prompt: In `return r -> this == r;`, `this` refers to the object whose method contains the lambda.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A lambda does not introduce its own `this`. It uses the lexically enclosing `this` context.

questions.prompt: A method returns a lambda that uses the local parameter `word`. What condition must `word` satisfy?

options.text: `word` must be a primitive type.
`word` must be `final` or effectively final.
`word` must be `null` after the method returns.
`word` must be an instance field.

questions.explanation: A captured parameter or local variable must not be reassigned after initialization. It may be explicitly `final` or remain effectively final.

questions.prompt: An anonymous subclass of `StoredValue` overrides `f()` with `return super.f() + 1;`. `StoredValue.f()` returns `x`, and `x` is `42`. What does the overriding method return?

questions.prompt: A lambda captures a local variable. Even if the same value is assigned to it again later, it is no longer effectively final.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Effectively final requires that there be no reassignment after initialization. The reassigned value does not have to be different for the rule to be violated.

questions.explanation: A lambda expression separates its parameters from its body with `->`. Here, the body directly returns the Boolean expression.

questions.prompt: Which statements about lambda syntax are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Parentheses are required for multiple parameters.

An expression body for a method with a return value must always also contain `return`.
Parentheses are optional for a single inferred parameter.

questions.prompt: An anonymous class extends the abstract class `AbstractValue`, whose constructor is `AbstractValue(int x)`. Which statement about creating an instance is correct?

The value can be passed to the superclass constructor when the object is created.

questions.prompt: A `default` method in a functional interface is already implemented and therefore does not count as a second abstract method requirement.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The method with a body is already implemented. The SAM property is determined by the number of abstract method requirements.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly compare anonymous classes and lambdas? Select all that apply.

options.text: An anonymous class can extend an abstract class.
A lambda can declare its own instance fields.
An anonymous class can implement multiple independent abstract methods.
Both can implement a functional interface.
A lambda can be declared as its own class with an explicit class name.

questions.explanation: Anonymous classes can implement interfaces with multiple methods or extend classes. Lambdas are designed for functional interfaces and do not declare their own instance fields or named classes.

questions.prompt: A lambda expression uses a local reference variable `items`. The reference is never reassigned, but an array element in the referenced array is changed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Changing the array automatically reassigns the local reference.
Capturing is forbidden because arrays must always be immutable.
Capturing is allowed only if the array is `null`.
Capturing is allowed if `items` is effectively final.

questions.explanation: Effectively final applies to the reference variable: it must not be reassigned. Changes to the referenced object are separate and may be allowed.

questions.prompt: A lambda can capture a local variable even if it is reassigned after initialization, as long as the new value is the same.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Any reassignment violates effectively final, even if the same value is assigned. The compiler reports the error before runtime.

questions.prompt: Which statements about functional interfaces are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A functional interface can also contain implemented methods.
A `default` method body makes it a second abstract method requirement.
The one abstract method requirement can have multiple parameters.
An interface with two independent abstract methods is still a target type for a lambda.
A lambda needs a target type that specifies its abstract method.

questions.explanation: SAM refers to a single abstract method requirement, not a single parameter. Implemented methods are allowed, and the target type provides the compiler with the method contract for the lambda.

questions.prompt: Why can `var p = r -> r != null;` not determine the lambda's type?

options.text: Because every lambda expression requires a block body.
Because `var` can store only primitive types.
Because the lambda lacks a target type from which its parameter and return types can be inferred.
Because lambdas can never be assigned to a variable.

questions.explanation: In this context, a lambda does not have a type without context. A target type such as `Property` specifies which method is implemented and which types apply.

questions.prompt: An object of `StringSearch` has the field `matchNull = false`. Its method `matching(String word)` returns a test that checks `word.equals(r) || (matchNull && r == null)`. Which statements about `word` and `matchNull` are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: `matchNull` is an instance field of the enclosing object.
Each created test necessarily gets its own copy of `matchNull`.
`matchNull` must be effectively final.
A call to `allowNulls()` that sets `matchNull` to `true` can affect existing tests.
`word` comes from the method parameter and is captured by each test.

questions.explanation: Each test captures its local `word`, but reads `matchNull` through the same enclosing object. Therefore, a later change to the field can change the behavior of tests that have already been created.

questions.prompt: What do the three test calls print, in order?

options.text: `false false true`
`true false true`
`true true false`
`false true false`

questions.explanation: For `null`, `&&` stops after the left-hand expression, so no cast is performed and the result is `false`. The integer `4` is even; `5` is not.

questions.prompt: When a lambda captures a `String` parameter, a deep copy of the `String` object is necessarily stored.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: For a reference type, the captured value is the reference. The notes explicitly distinguish between a reference and a deep copy of the referenced object.

questions.prompt: `StringSearch search` returns `p = search.matching("bye")` and `q = search.matching("hello")`. `matching` checks `word.equals(r) || (matchNull && r == null)`. Then `search.allowNulls()` is called; this method sets `matchNull` to `true`. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: `p.test("hello")` returns `true`.
`q.test(null)` returns `true`.
`p.test(null)` returns `true`.
`allowNulls()` changes the word captured by each test.
Both tests read the current field `matchNull` of the same object.

questions.explanation: `allowNulls()` sets the shared field to `true`, so both tests accept `null`. `p` still retains its captured word `bye` and does not thereby accept the string `hello`.

questions.prompt: Why is `new Property()` invalid without a class body following it?

options.text: Because every interface name requires a parameter.
Because a method `test` cannot have parameters.
Because `new` can only be used with primitive types.
Because `Property` is an interface, and the object can only be created through a concrete implementation.

questions.explanation: An interface is not a concrete class type that can be instantiated directly. Here, the anonymous class body provides an implementation whose object can be created.

questions.prompt: A `StringSearch` has the field `matchNull = false`. It creates `p = search.matching("bye")`, where `matching` returns a test for `word.equals(r) || (matchNull && r == null)`. Then `search.allowNulls()` is called, setting `matchNull` to `true`. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: `p.test(null)` returns `true`.
The test reads the current value of the field `matchNull` on every call.
`p.test("hello")` returns `true`.
`p.test("bye")` returns `true`.
The word captured by `p` is changed to `null` by `allowNulls()`.

questions.explanation: The test retains the captured word `bye`, but reads the mutable field `matchNull` when called. Therefore, after `allowNulls()`, both `bye` and `null` are accepted, but `hello` is not.

questions.explanation: The lambda uses the enclosing `this`, which is `owner`. The comparison `lambda.test(owner)` therefore compares the same reference with itself. The anonymous object, by contrast, uses its own `this`.

questions.prompt: A variable of type `Property` refers to an object of a concrete implementation that overrides `test`. Which implementation runs when `p.test(x)` is called?

options.text: None, because interface references cannot be used to call methods.
The implementation of the actual object that overrides `test`.
Always an implementation from `Object`.
The method is selected based on the variable name `p`.

questions.explanation: The reference type permits a call to `test`; for an overridden instance method, the actual object's class determines which implementation runs. This is dynamic binding.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?

options.text: `true true`
`false true`
`true false`
`false false`

questions.explanation: `r != null` is false on the first call; because of short-circuit evaluation, the right-hand expression is not evaluated and the cast to `Integer` is skipped. For the value `6`, the left-hand expression is true, and `6 % 2 == 0` is also true.

questions.prompt: Two different references `a` and `b` point to distinct objects with the same content; a suitable `equals` method checks that content. Which statement is correct?

options.text: `a == b` is `true` because the contents are equal.
`a == b` is `false`, while `a.equals(b)` can be `true`.
`==` and `equals` always check the same thing for references.
`a.equals(b)` must be `false` if the references are different.

questions.explanation: For references, `==` checks object identity. A suitable `equals` method can instead check value equality, so distinct objects can be equal in content.

questions.prompt: Which statements about anonymous classes and lambdas are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An anonymous class can implement an interface with multiple independent abstract methods.
Both can capture local values from the enclosing method call.
A lambda has its own `this` context.
A lambda can extend a concrete class.
An anonymous class can declare its own instance fields.

questions.explanation: Anonymous classes can define their own methods and fields and are not limited to functional interfaces. Both forms can capture local values if they are final or effectively final; however, a lambda does not introduce its own `this`.

questions.prompt: Why is `var p = r -> r != null;` not a valid replacement for `Property p = r -> r != null;`?

options.text: In `var`, the target type that specifies the lambda contract and parameter types is missing.
`Property` can only be used as a parameter, never as a variable type.
A lambda cannot contain a Boolean expression.
The name `p` is not allowed as a Java variable name.

questions.explanation: The lambda expression requires a known target type. `Property` provides the signature of `test`; without this context, the compiler cannot infer the lambda's type.

questions.prompt: A lambda can serve as an implementation for an interface with two independent abstract methods, provided both methods have the same return type.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A lambda supplies behavior for exactly one abstract method requirement. Two independent abstract methods mean the interface is not a functional interface, even if their return types are the same.

questions.prompt: A functional interface has exactly one abstract ___, which a lambda implements.

options.text: method requirement
instance variable
class declaration
constructor chaining

questions.explanation: The SAM property refers to a single abstract method requirement. Its parameter count can still be greater than one.

questions.prompt: A search algorithm should use the same loop for rules such as “not `null`” and “equal to a particular word.” Which design makes this possible?

options.text: Build a completely separate loop into the algorithm for each rule.
Store the rule implementation in each element of the array.
The interface must sort the array values before the search.
The algorithm handles the traversal; a passed `Property` implementation handles the rule.

questions.explanation: The algorithm stays the same for all rules and calls the passed test method for each element. This passes behavior as a parameter while keeping traversal separate from the selection rule.

source.heading: 1. Passing a matching rule – Verhalten übergeben

questions.prompt: You are building a Java route-planning app. The same loop should check candidate routes, but depending on the user's preference it should find either an accessible route or a route under 20 minutes. Which design fits this problem?

options.text: The loop always selects the first route without evaluating a selection rule.
The loop traverses the routes; the caller passes a `Property` with the desired selection rule.
Java must rewrite the loop's source code at runtime to use a different selection rule.
The `Property` itself determines which element the loop traverses next, making a loop unnecessary.

questions.explanation: The traversal stays the same, while the passed `Property` determines what counts as a match. This passes behavior as a parameter.

questions.prompt: A Java app should perform an action when the user clicks “Save Draft.” The button API expects a listener interface with exactly one abstract method. Which solution uses a lambda appropriately?

options.text: The listener interface must be an abstract class for a lambda to be used with it.
Use a lambda to fully implement an interface with two abstract methods.
Pass `event -> saveDraft()` directly as behavior in the button call.
Pass the lambda to the button API as a text string.

questions.explanation: The listener interface has one abstract method and can therefore serve as the target type for a lambda. The lambda supplies the action to perform on a click.

questions.prompt: A map app checks 30 routes in array order. The first match is at index 8 (counting starts at 0), and the search stops immediately when a match is found. How many calls to `Property.test` are made?
questions.explanation: Indices 0 through 8 are checked, for a total of 9 elements. The search ends immediately when a match is found at index 8.

questions.prompt: A game sensor needs a one-off implementation to handle two events (`onHit` and `onReset`) and store its own hit counter. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: A `default` method that stores a separate counter for each sensor object.
A captured local counter that is reassigned on every hit.
A single lambda that automatically implements both abstract methods.
An anonymous class that implements both methods and has its own counter field.

questions.explanation: An anonymous class can implement multiple abstract methods and have its own fields. A lambda implements the single abstract method of a functional interface.

questions.prompt: A messaging app schedules a notification for later. The method that schedules it ends first, but the later callback should still use the `messageId` passed in when it was scheduled. Which concept makes this possible?

options.text: The notification must read an instance field of the messaging app instead of the parameter.
The callback automatically accesses the latest value of any local variable that can be reassigned.
The compiler keeps the entire stack of the completed method in memory indefinitely.
The callback captures the parameter `messageId`; it must be final or effectively final.

questions.explanation: A callback can capture a local parameter and continue to use its value after the method ends. Captured local variables must not be reassigned.

source.heading: 3.2 Warum funktioniert der Test nach dem Methodenende?

questions.prompt: A playlist contains 40 entries, and exactly one matches the search. Assuming the matching entry is equally likely to be at any position and the search stops when it finds the match, how many calls to `Property.test` are made on average?
questions.explanation: Each hit position is equally likely, corresponding to between 1 and 40 calls. The mean is $(1+40)/2=20{,}5$.

questions.prompt: A dashboard filter is created in a controller method. Its rule reads the instance field `selectedCategory` of the same controller each time it checks an item. Later, the user changes the category, and the already-created filter should use the new selection. What describes this behavior?

options.text: The compiler replaces the filter with an anonymous class after every change.
The filter captured the field value as a local variable, which is automatically reassigned when the field changes.
The filter reads the controller's current enclosing state on each call.
The annotation `@FunctionalInterface` automatically makes the field mutable.

questions.explanation: The instance field is read through the enclosing controller object. Therefore, changes to `selectedCategory` can affect the behavior of a filter that has already been created.

source.heading: 4. Enclosing state – Zustand des umgebenden Objekts

questions.prompt: You are writing a test generator for a four-digit PIN. Each digit can be from 0 to 9, and leading zeros are allowed. How many different candidates can a `Property` potentially check, in thousands?
questions.explanation: Each of the four digits has 10 possibilities, so there are $10^4=10\,000$ candidates. That is 10 thousand PINs that a passed rule could check.

questions.prompt: In an instance method of a Java controller, you pass `event -> this.refresh()` as a click action. Which statement about `this` is correct?

options.text: `this` refers to the controller whose method contains the lambda.
`this` refers to an automatically generated anonymous class object.
A lambda can use `this` only if the controller is a functional interface.
`this` always refers to the object currently invoking the click action.

questions.explanation: A lambda does not introduce its own `this`; it uses the lexically enclosing context. Here, that is the controller.

questions.prompt: A network parser checks a packet using `packet != null && packet.isValid()`. Which everyday situation demonstrates short-circuit behavior here?

options.text: The compiler caches the result of `isValid()` for later packets.
Both sides of `&&` are always evaluated, regardless of the left-hand result.
If `packet` is `null`, `packet.isValid()` is not called.
The parser skips `packet.isValid()` for every other packet.

questions.explanation: With `&&`, the right-hand side is evaluated only if the left-hand side is `true`. This means that when `packet == null`, no method call on `null` is attempted.
